tldr: The authors turned real furnished homes into studios to build "ACE-Data-0," a 150-hour dataset that fully synchronizes egocentric/exocentric video, whole-body and hand mocap, 6-DoF object trajectories, tactile signals, and audio down to the millisecond. Evaluating over 30 state-of-the-art models revealed that existing methods break down significantly under real-world occlusions and long-horizon cumulative drift.
hero_caption: The overall workflow of ACE. Participants wear mocap suits and tactile gloves to perform daily tasks. After capture, an optical clock and other tools strictly synchronize timelines across all modalities, automatically generating high-precision annotations directly grounded in physical measurements.
overview:
Casual human daily actions—like opening a door, pouring water into a glass, and carrying it—tightly integrate perception, whole-body coordination, dexterous manipulation, and tactile feedback. However, for embodied AI to acquire these skills, physical interaction data cannot simply be scraped from the web; it must be gathered from scratch. Most existing datasets have been limited to simplistic laboratory settings, fragmented viewpoints and modalities, or brief isolated actions lasting only a few seconds.

To address this, the authors developed the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE), which transforms real-life living spaces—complete with furniture and daily items—into full-scale capture studios. ACE features two complementary setups: a table-scale configuration to capture fine finger manipulation, and a room-scale configuration to record whole-body locomotion across entire rooms. It completely synchronizes egocentric (Ego) video, multi-view exocentric (Exo) video, whole-body and hand skeletons, 6-DoF object poses, tactile signals, and audio into a single spatial-temporal coordinate system with millisecond precision.

Using this system, the team built "ACE-Data-0," capturing 200 goal-oriented tasks across 50 participants, totaling 150 hours, 17 million frames, and 75,000 episodes. They also established a three-tier hierarchical benchmark spanning low-level signals (tactile estimation from video), scene components (whole-body pose estimation), and interactions (hand motion estimation), evaluating more than 30 representative methods.

Results revealed that state-of-the-art models—despite high accuracy in lab environments—degraded sharply due to lower-body occlusions from furniture, egomotion estimation errors from rapid head movements, and cumulative drift across long task horizons. This demonstrates that physically grounded data, genuinely synchronized in time and space, is indispensable for training foundational models for real-world robotics.
contributions: Built the capture system "ACE," which turns real, furnished residential spaces into recording environments and fully synchronizes multi-view video, full-body/hand mocap, 6-DoF object poses, tactile signals, and audio across table-scale and room-scale setups.

Released "ACE-Data-0," a large-scale, long-horizon interaction dataset consisting of 150 hours and 75,000 episodes, capturing natural planning and trial-and-error driven by goal-level rather than step-by-step instructions.
Automatically generated 2D/3D annotations robust to occlusions and motion blur by reprojecting high-precision measured tracking data, without relying on error-prone predictive pipelines.

Evaluated over 30 state-of-the-art methods across three tiers (signals, components, and interactions), systematically exposing key challenges and failure modes unique to long-horizon tasks in real home environments.

sections.heading: Why physical embodied data cannot be gathered from the web
sections.summary: Unlike large language models, training data for embodied intelligence cannot be crawled online and must be recorded from the physical world. Existing datasets suffer from fragmented modalities, artificial lab settings, and short task durations. To overcome these limits, the authors propose ACE, a data engine for multimodal synchronized capture in real homes, and the ACE-Data-0 dataset.
sections.details:
Humans naturally coordinate perception, whole-body movement, fine manipulation, and touch while surrounded by furniture and everyday household objects. Unlike text and 2D images, tacit physical skills—such as how firmly to grasp a cup, or how to coordinate gaze and balance—have never been documented as text in human history. Advancing embodied AI therefore requires data engines that blanket real living spaces with sensors to record physical interactions as they happen.

However, existing datasets face three major barriers:
- Fragmented modalities: Large-scale egocentric datasets like Ego4D capture natural human behavior but lack ground-truth 3D motion for whole bodies and objects. Conversely, mocap datasets like BEHAVE provide accurate body skeletons but omit egocentric views, touch, and audio.
- Artificial environments: Most studies capturing accurate geometric ground truth operate in clean, empty laboratories, stripping away realistic furniture occlusions, clutter, and spatial constraints.
- Short horizons: Most existing datasets focus on isolated actions lasting a few seconds (e.g., picking and placing), omitting long-horizon activities lasting tens of minutes where multiple sub-tasks are chained while moving through a home.

This work introduces the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE), turning real homes into capture studios without sacrificing everyday realism. ACE combines a table-scale setup for fine hand manipulation and a room-scale setup for whole-body movement and furniture contact, fusing all sensors into a unified spatial-temporal coordinate system. Using this setup, the authors collected ACE-Data-0 (150 hours, 75,000 episodes) and created a three-tier benchmark to measure the true capabilities of perception and action models in real-world conditions.

sections.heading: Positioning within multimodal, egocentric, and long-horizon research
sections.summary: Prior works focused on local hand grasping, egocentric video, or long-horizon tasks in isolation, but none captured whole-body motion, first-person views, touch, and object tracking along a single timeline. ACE-Data-0 bridges these domains, combining natural human behavioral structure with rigorous physical measurement.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main streams:

### 2.1 Multimodal Datasets and Benchmarks
Early physically grounded datasets (such as ContactPose, DexYCB, and H2O) concentrated primarily on local hand-object contact and mesh poses. Subsequent datasets scaled up to whole-body interactions (BEHAVE, GRAB), bimanual manipulation hierarchies (OakInk2), or dense multi-camera capture using 51 cameras (GigaHands). However, these setups either remain confined to table surfaces or capture whole-body movement while sacrificing egocentric viewpoints and tactile feedback. ACE-Data-0 differs fundamentally by capturing multimodal streams—including touch and audio—as unified physical events through a shared calibration and synchronization pipeline.

### 2.2 Egocentric Datasets and Transfer to Robot Learning
Ego4D and Ego-Exo4D established the scale and diversity of first-person perspectives, inspiring recent efforts like DexMV and EgoVLA to learn robot policies directly from human egocentric video. However, they lack continuous ground truth for long-horizon full-body skeletons and 6-DoF object trajectories. Meanwhile, teleoperation datasets (such as Fourier ActionNet) provide direct robot control signals but remain bound to specific robot embodiments. ACE-Data-0 pairs wearable cameras with ground-truth body and object tracking, providing embodiment-agnostic egocentric experiences.

### 2.3 Long-Horizon Interactions
Everyday household tasks feature long temporal dependencies: past actions restrict future choices, and people must track intermediate states while moving across rooms. Recent robot learning benchmarks (Mobile ALOHA, AgiBot World) tackle long tasks, but primarily score end-to-end success, making it hard to diagnose whether failures stem from missed contact, state estimation drift, or planning errors. ACE-Data-0 encourages natural trial and error via unscripted, goal-level prompts and records the entire process multimodally, enabling detailed failure attribution.

sections.heading: System design: Turning a furnished home into a capture space
sections.summary: To resolve the trade-off between local fingertip contact and room-wide navigation, ACE adopts two setups: table-scale (30 m²) and room-scale (a 200 m² furnished apartment). Strategically placed egocentric fisheye cameras, exocentric static cameras, OptiTrack mocap, and tactile gloves eliminate blind spots across all modalities.
sections.details:
Completely capturing real-world interactions requires tracking both sub-millimeter fingertip contacts and meter-scale movements across rooms. Because no single setup can satisfy both, ACE implements two complementary scales.

### 3.1 System Overview
- Table-scale: A 30 m² workspace centered around a workbench. It employs 8 close-range GoPro cameras (0.3 to 0.5 m away), 16 OptiTrack PrimeX 22 cameras mounted on an overhead truss, and high-density tactile gloves to capture fine bimanual manipulation at sub-millimeter effective resolution.
- Room-scale: A ~200 m² furnished apartment including a kitchen, dining area, living room, and bedroom. An overhead truss suspends 8 wide-baseline ZED One RGB cameras (mounted on telescoping poles to clear blind spots) and 12 OptiTrack cameras, ensuring participants remain visible to at least 4 cameras anywhere in the home despite furniture occlusions.

### 3.2 Hardware Configuration
- Egocentric cameras: Participants wear the "ACE-Ego-Head-V02 Lite" headset (featuring four fisheye cameras pointing front, back, left, and right, capturing 1088x1280 resolution at 20 FPS, with an onboard IMU). Five mocap markers mounted on the headset continuously track 6-DoF head pose.
- Exocentric cameras: 8 GoPros (1080p, 30 FPS) are used for table-scale, and 8 GMSL2-connected ZED One cameras (1080p, 30 FPS) cover the room-scale setup.
- Human and hand motion: Participants wear a 41-marker suit tracked by OptiTrack at 60 Hz for whole-body skeletons. Hand joints are captured at 60 Hz using Manus mocap gloves in the room-scale setup, and via multi-view triangulation with manual refinement in the table-scale setup.
- Object motion: Everyday items are pre-scanned using 3D scanners or 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) to create accurate meshes. Multiple rigid markers attached to each object track 6-DoF poses at 60 Hz.
- Tactile and audio: Full-palm tactile gloves record contact pressure distributions across palms and fingers, while microphones on the GoPros and headset record contact sounds and ambient audio.

captions.F2: Overall layout of the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE). On the left, the room-scale setup (a 200 m² apartment) minimizes blind spots with truss-mounted cameras; on the right, the table-scale setup captures fine hand manipulation with close-up cameras and tactile sensors.

sections.heading: Millisecond synchronization and ground-truth annotations
sections.summary: Heterogeneous sensor streams are synchronized to millisecond accuracy using an optical clock (reading nanosecond screen QR codes), and spatially calibrated via ArUco boards despite non-overlapping fields of view. The team recorded 150 hours of natural, long-horizon behavior across 50 participants, labeled with high-quality annotations projected directly from physical tracking.
sections.details:
Here is the pipeline used to integrate over 10 different sensor streams, along with key dataset details.

### 4.1 Data Acquisition Pipeline (Synchronization and Calibration)
- Temporal synchronization: Network synchronization alone cannot resolve exposure offsets (causing ~0.29 s delays and drift). The team developed an "optical clock" approach: the mocap workstation displays a nanosecond-precision clock as a dynamic QR code, which external cameras record directly. Linear interpolation keeps final sync errors within one mocap frame (a few milliseconds or less). Egocentric cameras achieve sync by glancing at the screen at the start of a session, while tactile gloves synchronize through a dedicated IMU gesture matching pattern where participants move head and hands simultaneously.
- Spatial calibration: Room-scale exocentric cameras share almost no visual overlap. The team used an ArUco board fitted with retroreflective markers at its corners, visible to both RGB and infrared mocap cameras simultaneously, placing all cameras into a shared OptiTrack world coordinate frame. For the egocentric camera, tracking rigid markers on the headset and solving Hand-Eye Calibration produces drift-free 6-DoF camera poses for every frame without relying on visual odometry.

### 4.2 Data Collection and Task Design
Discarding rigid, scripted instructions, participants received only abstract, goal-level prompts such as "make tea and bring it to the table." This naturally preserved hesitation, replanning, and personal variation in navigation paths.
- Atomic HOI tasks (~3 minutes): Over 15 short-horizon skills, including pouring, cooking, and wiping.
- HOI chain tasks (20–30 minutes): Complete daily activity cycles chaining multiple short tasks, concluding with tidying up the room.
- Human-Scene Interaction (HSI) tasks (~5 minutes): Whole-body contact with furniture, such as sitting on chairs, lounging on sofas, walking, and exercising.

### 4.3 Automated Annotation Generation
Spanning 50 participants and 150 hours (17 million frames, 75,000 episodes), the dataset includes five label types. Crucially, except for language descriptions (generated by Gemini-3.1-pro-preview and human-verified), all annotations—2D/3D human poses, 6-DoF object bounding boxes and trajectories, and tactile contact—are generated via **direct geometric reprojection from physical measurements**, rather than inferred by pretrained models. As a result, labels remain reliable even under severe occlusions and motion blur.

sections.heading: Real-world hurdles break over 30 state-of-the-art models
sections.summary: Existing models were benchmarked across tactile estimation, whole-body pose estimation, and hand motion estimation. Accurately localizing contact from video remains difficult. Furthermore, while models can estimate local joint angles reasonably well, real-world long-horizon tracking and egomotion estimation suffer severe cumulative errors.
sections.details:
The benchmark mirrors the perceptual hierarchy of humans and robots across three levels, evaluated on a 10-hour test set.

### 5.1 Low-Level Signals: Tactile Estimation from Video
This task requires estimating contact pressure distributions across palms and fingers from egocentric video. Three methods were evaluated: PressureVision, EgoPressureDiff, and TouchAnything. While TouchAnything—pretrained on large-scale vision-tactile data—performed best, its Contact IoU (contact area overlap) and Volumetric IoU (matching pressure magnitude) remained modest, with persistent Center of Pressure (CoP) errors. While models can detect contact presence (timing), determining exactly where and how much pressure is applied when hands and objects occlude each other remains exceptionally challenging.

### 5.2 Scene Components: Whole-Body Motion Estimation
In the room-scale setup, models estimated 3D whole-body skeletons from long videos containing furniture occlusions and crouching. The benchmark compared 22 approaches across monocular, multi-view, egocentric, and scene-aware methods.
- Local pose vs. global trajectory: Most monocular methods achieved respectable local joint errors after Procrustes alignment (PA-MPJPE), close to standard benchmark performance. However, world-aligned trajectory errors (WA-MPJPE) exploded. While per-frame joint articulation was estimated reasonably well, global navigation paths through the room drifted severely.
- The impact of scene geometry: Scene-aware methods (such as UniSH and JOSH) showed local pose accuracy comparable to pure video baselines, but significantly reduced global trajectory error. The 3D geometry of the room provided strong physical constraints on where a person can stand.
- Viewpoint differences: Egocentric methods (like EgoEgo) lost sight of the lower body, relying heavily on head motion cues and performing substantially worse than exocentric approaches.

### 5.3 Body Interactions: Hand Motion Estimation
For hand manipulation, identical movements were estimated and compared from both egocentric (WildHands, Dyn-HaMR, HaWoR) and exocentric viewpoints (HaMeR, WiLoR, HaPTIC).
- Challenges of egocentric views: While single-frame methods (WildHands) captured local finger configurations well (low PA-MPJPE), estimating global hand trajectories from video produced errors near 100 mm. Rapid head motion introduced camera egomotion errors that directly disrupted global hand placement.
- Advantages of exocentric views: Static third-person methods (HaPTIC) struggled with smaller hand pixel sizes and object occlusions, but their fixed spatial reference frame kept global trajectory errors down to 63 mm.
These findings highlight the need for cross-view approaches that blend the close-up detail of egocentric cameras with the stable reference frames of exocentric views.

sections.heading: New horizons unlocked by embodied data engines
sections.summary: The authors introduced ACE, an engine that turns real living spaces into fully synchronized capture studios, and released the 150-hour ACE-Data-0 dataset. Benchmarks revealed key weaknesses in existing perception models under real-world conditions, paving the way for using this data directly to train imitation learning, world models, and vision-language-action (VLA) systems.
sections.details:
This study introduced the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE), capturing multimodal signals synchronized to millisecond precision while preserving natural behavior in home settings, and released ACE-Data-0 (150 hours, 75,000 episodes). A three-tier benchmark revealed that real-world factors—such as contact estimation, furniture occlusions, and long-horizon egomotion drift—remain major stumbling blocks for current methods.

The core value of this dataset lies not just in evaluation, but in its utility as direct training data for robots. Synchronizing egocentric video, multi-view exocentric video, accurate 3D motion trajectories, and contact ground truth provides an ideal training signal for imitation learning, policy learning, world models, and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.

### Limitations and Future Work
The authors note several limitations:
- Environmental diversity: Data was gathered across two physical environments (30 m² and 200 m²), limiting variation in room layouts and lighting.
- Object scope: Tracking is currently restricted to pre-scanned rigid and articulated objects with attached markers; deformable objects like cloth, fluids, and internal mechanical state changes are not yet annotated.
- Visual artifacts from wearable gear: Mocap suits, gloves, headsets, and markers remain visible in the video, which could introduce unwanted visual biases for downstream vision models.

takeaways: In long-horizon home tasks, even if per-frame local body and hand pose estimation is accurate, global trajectory estimation in world coordinates still drifts and breaks down due to cumulative errors.

Egocentric views provide valuable close-up details of hands, but egomotion errors caused by rapid head movements directly disrupt hand trajectories, making fusion with exocentric views and scene geometry crucial.

Reconstructing accurate contact pressure distributions (tactile signals) purely from video remains difficult even for modern diffusion models, underscoring the need for multimodal physical ground-truth supervision.
Training embodied AI for robotics requires moving beyond scraping isolated video clips toward unified data engines where all sensor modalities are physically grounded along the exact same timeline.
limitations: Recordings were conducted in only two residential environments, limiting diversity in floor plans, furniture designs, and lighting conditions.
Tracked objects are restricted to pre-scanned, marker-equipped rigid and articulated items, leaving liquids, soft materials, and deformable items like cloth unannotated.
Wearable gear—including mocap suits, tactile gloves, and optical markers—is visible in camera feeds, potentially introducing unnatural visual biases for image recognition models.
